corrections.form_value: Study A: analyzed arm counts 24, 21, 16, 12, 6 and total 79; Study B: 16, 16, 16 and total 48 including the shared neutral arm; Study C: 16, 16 and total 32 including the shared standard-model arm. The participant descriptions say the reported condition counts are used for both assignment and analysis.
corrections.source_says: The condition-specific human counts occur in the random-assignment paragraph. No separate final analyzed human counts or post-assignment participant-flow accounting are reported. The form correctly discloses that its study totals are arithmetic sums, but equality of allocated and analyzed samples is not explicitly established. Set arm-level and study-level n_analyzed to null and describe post-assignment exclusions as not stated; retain the printed allocation counts and identify any summed totals as calculations. Methods M1 defines consensus over all members of a group of 24 humans and agents; that mathematical definition does not independently establish the human analyzed sample or absence of attrition.
corrections.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of eight experimental conditions spanning three studies.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 16, Supplementary Information, Experimental Procedure, Participants; p. 7, Methods M1, Consensus strength. No separate analyzed human counts are given elsewhere in the complete 29-page PDF.

corrections.form_value: criterion_2_at_least_50_people = met; the reason uses the calculated Study A total of 79 as sufficient to establish the participant threshold.
corrections.source_says: Use unclear for the threshold of at least 50 people analyzed, because the reported allocation counts do not separately confirm the final analyzed count. Study A has a calculated allocation total of 79 from the printed arm counts, so it remains a candidate for full screening. Studies B and C remain below 50 even if every allocated human is analyzed and the shared neutral comparator is included: their calculated comparison-sample maxima are 48 and 32, respectively. Keep core = unclear, context_class = none, and route the randomized people study to the two-screener pipeline.
corrections.quote: Study A examined the effect of agent proportion, with conditions at 0% (n = 24), 12.5% (n = 21), 33.3% (n = 16), 50% (n = 12), and 75% (n = 6) agent ratios.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 16, Supplementary Information, Experimental Procedure, Participants; form-spec.md, Field notes for eligibility.core (the threshold counts people analyzed).

confirmed: The source is arXiv:2609.02122v1 dated 2 September 2026, by Lin Chen, Ziyi Liu, Xia Hu, and Yong Li; the PDF has 29 pages and includes Supplementary Information on pp. 16-29 (PDF p. 1 version stamp and authors; p. 11 Additional information; pp. 16-29).

Random assignment of people to eight conditions spanning Studies A, B, and C is explicit, separately from random partner matching. The game uses a web-based experimental platform, supporting the online randomized-design classification and context_class = none; this is original experimental research rather than a synthesis, observational comparison, or AI-only output comparison (PDF p. 16, Participants and Game Procedure).

The paper reports 127 human recruits from universities in China. Study A lists human condition counts 24, 21, 16, 12, and 6; Study B lists 16 high-adoption and 16 high-persistence participants; Study C lists 16 smaller-model participants. These are people counts, not description, agent, or rating counts (PDF p. 16, Participants).

The form transparently derives 79 for Study A, 48 for the Study B comparison including the shared neutral condition, and 32 for Study C including the shared standard-model condition. These sums agree with the printed arm counts but are not separately printed study totals; the neutral/standard comparator must not be counted as new recruits in B and C (PDF p. 16, Participants; p. 4, trait and capability comparisons).

Study B and Study C are below the 50-person threshold even when their shared comparator is included and all allocated participants are assumed retained; only Study A can potentially meet it (PDF p. 16, condition counts; calculated comparison totals as described in the form).

Each session contains 24 players including humans and any AI agents, uses the same tangram across sessions, and lasts 40 rounds with a recommended response time of 60 seconds per round. Humans submit a single English sentence, receive their partner description afterward, and are told to refrain from external language-model assistance (PDF p. 16, Stimuli and Game Procedure).

The standard agent model is Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct and the smaller-model condition uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Neutral is the default game prompt; high-adoption and high-persistence prompts manipulate alignment with partners versus retaining prior wording (PDF p. 4, Results; p. 9, Methods M4; pp. 18-19, Agent Trait Prompts).

Consensus is scored on produced descriptions using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 cosine similarity: each member is compared with all other members, followed by within-individual centering and group aggregation at the final round. It includes agent-generated descriptions, so the form correctly cautions that this is not a human-only diversity contrast (PDF p. 7, Methods M1, equations 1-2).

Study A reported string is numerically correct: 33.3% agents has consensus 0.534 versus pure-human 0.695, with a reported 23.1% decrease, z = -12.326, p < 0.001 (PDF p. 2, Results; p. 4 supplies the 0.534 standard-model level; p. 12, Figure 1b).

Study B reported string is numerically correct: high persistence reduces consensus by 9.6% relative to neutral at 33.3% agents, z = -3.289, p = 0.001 (PDF p. 4, agent-trait manipulation results; p. 14, Figure 3d).

Study C reported string is numerically correct: the smaller model yields consensus 0.725 versus 0.534 for the standard model, z = 14.143, p < 0.001 (PDF p. 4, agent-capability comparison; p. 14, Figure 3f).

Every number in the one-line finding matches the PDF: pure-human consensus 0.695; an 8.0% increase at 12.5% agents; decreases of 23.1% and 14.5% at 33.3% and 50% agents; and consensus 0.725 at 75% agents. These are consensus/similarity results, with higher values indicating lower diversity (PDF p. 2, Results; p. 7, Methods M1; p. 12, Figure 1b).

The included supplement contains participant recruitment and allocation, prompts, contribution methods, robustness figures, and Supplementary Table 1 on adoption willingness. That table concerns self-reported willingness and HC3 regression uncertainty, not a pooled creativity effect; leaving the synthesis fields unfilled is appropriate (PDF pp. 16-29; p. 29, Supplementary Table 1).

The paper warrants the randomized-people flag for further review because people are assigned to different generative-AI partner conditions and their written outputs enter similarity scoring. The form appropriately retains scope questions about AI as a game partner and similarity across mixed human-AI groups (PDF p. 16, Participants and Game Procedure; p. 7, Methods M1).
summary: Random assignment, the source version, all three reported contrasts, and the one-line finding are confirmed against the PDF. The analyzed counts and resulting 50-person eligibility claim require qualification because separate analyzed human counts are not reported; retain this paper in the two-screener pipeline.
